items.title: Researchers Need to Learn How AI Makes Decisions, Says Goodfire’s Tom McGrath
items.summary:
To understand the decision-making of AI, developers often look at the text that models produce as they reason through problems. But these “chains of thought” are increasingly hard to read, which is prompting AI developers to consider other approaches. One alternative, known as “mechanistic interpretability,” seeks to explain the inner workings of AI models, rather than just relying on their outward behavior.

Leading AI companies have formed mechanistic interpretability teams in recent years, and the field has spawned several startups, the most prominent of which is Goodfire AI, whose chief scientist Tom McGrath joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode is available here.)

items.title: Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?
items.summary:
If it’s Monday, it must be time for another AI model release. This time, it was Meta Platforms’ turn, unveiling Muse Wonder, which it claims can “deliver state-of-the-art performance” on certain tasks. It was a triumphant moment for the company, whose AI efforts previously went through a slump that prompted a massive hiring binge over the past 14 months or so. It now claims it is “pushing the frontier” of AI.

That would be notable if only everyone wasn’t claiming to be doing the same thing. Two weeks ago, Google unveiled its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, which it says “delivers frontier performance in complex workflows” across various subjects (you wouldn’t want it to deliver frontier performance in simple workflows, would you?). In early September, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which it said was “state of the art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.” Also in September, Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, which it claimed to be “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.”

mentions.title: Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?
Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?

llm.summary: Meta Platforms recently launched Muse Wonder, an AI model it claims offers state-of-the-art performance on specific tasks. This release follows a period of intensified hiring and restructuring within Meta's AI division. However, the AI landscape is highly competitive, with other major companies like Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic also unveiling advanced AI models such as Google's Gemini 4 Argon, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, each highlighting their own cutting-edge capabilities. The crowded field raises questions about how users will differentiate and respond to these new AI offerings.

Earlier this year, the ChatGPT-maker canned both the model and the TikTok-like app it powered as part of broader culling of server-intensive “side projects” even as rivals xAI and Google forged ahead with their own video models.

Well, there’s a chance that a version of Sora is coming back from the dead.

A stealthy startup developing AI video for filmmakers, which we revealed last month, is in talks with OpenAI to access Sora, tweak it and sell software or other services using it, according to a person with knowledge of the talks. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg, former Sora research lead Bill Peebles, and former Dropbox CFO Sujay Jaswa co-founded the startup in recent months. (We don’t know the startup’s name).

items.title: Amazon’s Bargains Include Its Stock
items.summary:
It’s the quiet before the storm of earnings season, which starts in a week or two. While we wait for the third-quarter updates, here’s a thought: Investor enthusiasm for semiconductor stocks and blue-sky vision companies like SpaceX appears to have sucked money out of stocks of long-established tech companies. Some are now trading at bargain-basement prices. We’re thinking specifically of Amazon, whose stock really deserves a bit more love. 

We know the gripes: Like Alphabet and Meta, Amazon is spending an absolute ton—$220 billion this year alone—on capital expenditures to build out its AI data center capacity. That’s not without risk, for sure: The investment depends on business demand for AI services taking off. Even so, that can’t justify Amazon trading at a discount to Walmart, as it has done for the last 18 months or so. Walmart is expected to grow revenue this year by about 5.6%—about a third of Amazon’s estimated growth rate. And yet Amazon is trading at about 29 times forward earnings, compared with 37 times for Walmart, according to Koyfin data.

items.title: Zuckerberg’s Big Biotech Moment
items.summary:
• The Big Read: Meet Zach Frankel, the secretive investor behind Cognition, Ramp

• Why techies are hoarding AI compute in their homes

• Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “Bram Stoker’s Dracula,” “The AGI Chronicles” and “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”

Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, was only six years old in 1990, the year the Human Genome Project got launched.

That project, a multibillion-dollar international effort led by the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy, resulted in the announcement 10 years later of an awe-inspiring milestone: the first sequencing of the human genetic code—the building blocks of life. When President Bill Clinton described the achievement in 2000, he framed it in grand terms: “We are learning the language in which God created life.”

So it was intriguing to hear another scientific collaboration compared to that earlier achievement at a reception this week hosted by Biohub, the primary philanthropic effort of Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. The event this week is one of a number of recent moments that herald a changing of the scientific guard from major universities to big tech companies.  

Speaking at the Treehouse Hotel in Sunnyvale, Calif., Zuckerberg told the gathering of around 100 tech executives, scientists and academics that he and Chan had started the first version of what is now called Biohub almost 10 years ago to the day with the goal of trying to cure and prevent all diseases by the end of the century. “We got a lot of eye rolls,” Zuckerberg said. “People thought that was kind of crazy.” Thanks to AI and other advances in technology, he added, “That no longer seems quite so crazy.”

He then turned to Lori Goler, president of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, who announced that Biohub is partnering with the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy in a $1.8 billion investment to create new technologies and build the scientific infrastructure required to drive “AI-powered biology.” 

Biohub, which launched what it calls the “Virtual Biology Initiative” in April with a $500 million commitment, also said at the event that Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, a company spun off of DeepMind, have agreed to kick in $300 million.

“We were inspired by the Human Genome Project,” Goler told the group. Goler added that they hope the initiative “will have the same level of impact and will be as important as the Human Genome Project has been.” (Anyone going to The Information’s WTF Summit later this month will hear more from Goler on the future of AI biology.)

Despite the evening’s focus on collaboration, science can be an isolating discipline in its daily practice. When I visit labs, I am always amazed by how quiet they are. The scientists are usually intently concentrating on not making a false step that could lead to the contamination of an experiment. And yet, once the results leave the lab and reach the public, clamor often ensues. Controversial findings spark debate over ethical and moral questions. Transformative discoveries are celebrated with an element of pageantry and recognition. Both are reminders of our common humanity—and that the ultimate goal of science is to make all our lives better. This leads to invitations to the White House like the one that happened back in 2000 with the scientists at the helm of the Human Genome Project. Or even more personal celebratory videos like the ones posted on social media all this week by happy scientists who received early morning calls from Sweden learning they had won Nobel Prizes. (How can you not be moved by this video of the Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth telling his kids he won the Nobel Prize for medicine?)

Zuckerberg is one of the most prominent symbols of how AI is altering the scientific landscape and bringing new leaders into an arena once dominated by major universities.  He was appointed by President Trump in March to be a member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He is joined there by other high-profile Silicon Valley names, including Google’s Sergey Brin, Oracle’s Larry Ellison and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. Of the 13 people now on the council, only one is an academic researcher.

Two other signs this week reflect the change. On Oct. 8, Brin and Huang, alongside other tech notables, received the National Medals of Science from President Trump. The same day, Anthropic said it is expanding its own partnership with the government. It will provide $150 million worth of AI credits and other support for the Genesis Mission launched by Trump last year to use AI to accelerate scientific discoveries.

A Biohub team traveled to Washington in July to attend the first Genesis Mission Summit. Plans for the newly announced partnership with the National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy grew out of that visit. So perhaps it’s only fair that the government made its own pilgrimage out to Silicon Valley. Appearing on stage together is another way of showing a shared faith that Silicon Valley and AI are the favored engines these days to try to unlock insights into the mysteries of our cells and what goes wrong when we get sick.

I talked briefly with Goler the day after the reception. She said Biohub plans to host an annual AI and bio event. Biohub will likely find more guests eager to attend, from the private sector and the government. “It really is a cultural moment,” she said.—Amy Dockser Marcus (amy.marcus@theinformation.com) 

Weekend’s Latest Stories

The Big Read

Shroud of Secrecy Cloaks Star Investor Behind Cognition, Ramp

While an air of mystery hangs around Zach Frankel, he has picked up stakes in some of tech's buzziest companies and established an extensive web of connections.

The GPUs in the Wine Cellar

Techies are tricking out their homes with powerful AI computers. Then come the heat issues.

Listening: “Bram Stoker’s Dracula”

How do you give, uh, fresh life to Bram Stoker’s classic? Filling it up with an all-star cast of film actors sure works. In Audible’s new adaptation of “Dracula,” Jonathan Bailey is the undead count; Maggie Gyllenhaal is Van Helsing, the occult expert who leads the expedition to destroy the vampire; and Ella Purnell (from “Fallout” and “Yellowjackets”) is Mina, a character reimagined from Stoker’s original from hapless victim into the story’s central protagonist. 

Thanks to its Amazon budget, Audible clearly spared no expense: the sound production is top-notch and directing duties of the audio dramatization went to Mary Lambert, a Hollywood veteran best known for her 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King’s “Pet Sematary.” —Abram Brown

Reading: “The AGI Chronicles” by Kevin Roose

How exactly did we get here—to this moment in time with AIs that increasingly seem human absolutely everywhere? And that’s to say nothing of the endless hand-wringing about whether they’re actually going to end all of us humans. 

A rather definitive answer to that question lies in “The AGI Chronicles,” a colorful, insidery account of the tech industry’s rapacious quest to develop artificial general intelligence. Or, as author Kevin Roose terms it, “the strangest decade in our history.” Roose, the former New York Times technology columnist, begins in the 2010s, a period when creating human-like AI was seen as something “between a pipe dream and a fantasy,” he writes, though a few people who are now bold-faced names wanted to give it a shot: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis among them. Of course, what looked like a quixotic endeavor then quickly morphed into the multitrillion-dollar competition that currently surrounds us. 

As Roose charts the twists and turns, he includes many little details to love. Just before Altman, Oracle’s Larry Ellison and President Donald Trump announced Project Stargate in January 2025, Altman had to send a last-minute text message to Jeff Bezos to make sure they could use that name for their massive data center initiative: Bezos’s Amazon owns MGM, and MGM owns the rights to the “Stargate” TV-and-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Google’s Gemini was almost called Titan—a Hassabis suggestion—but company lawyers vetoed the name as “too aggressive.” And when Daniela Amodei worked at OpenAI, she and her husband, an early OpenAI board member, used a large collection of stuffed animals as their “personal advisory council,” as Roose puts it. (That detail went viral a bit last week from an early excerpt of the book.) 

From “The AGI Chronicles,” what I was struck by most is how the AI race has warped its contestants and magnified their worst tendencies. I expect that trend will continue. It’s not as if they’ll be facing any less pressure anytime soon. According to Roose, many of those titans echoed the same sentiment in conversations with him—that they “missed their old lives, and they relished the times when everyone thought they were crazy for believing that AGI was possible,” he writes. “Being an underdog, they said, was more fun than being a power broker, with all the scrutiny and skepticism it brought.”—A.B.

Watching: “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”

By actor Mahershala Ali’s own telling, the past few years have been challenging, with his fate skewed by other forces that have defied his control, including Marvel’s decision to shelve his reboot of “Blade,” its half-vampire vampire slayer. 

“I think in some ways I’m probably just now starting to let certain things go, because there are ways in which I think I’ve begun to let go of my expectations of the world and the business,” Ali said in a recent GQ interview to promote his new film, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” “It’s like you’re fighting with people to see you how you see yourself.”

I can see how Ali’s own real-life wrestling with his identity and fate might’ve fueled his interest in doing “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” His character in the film, a mournful hitman named Latif, faces those same challenges—as he tries to extricate himself from a dingy Houston underworld and take up single-parent duties to his three children. Complicating that escape is a gangster pastor (John Cho) and his mobster former employer (Laith Nakli). The thriller-ish drama is punctuated by several balletic action sequences, all deftly handled by newcomer director Bassam Tariq, who’d been attached to helm the “Blade” reboot with Ali. If nothing else, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” is a sharp jab to Marvel’s ribs: Tariq and Ali seem like they would’ve made a terrific “Blade” together.—A.B.

items.title: GPUs in the Wine Cellar: Why Techies Are Hoarding AI Compute in Their Homes
items.summary:
The basement of Gary Flake’s contemporary home in a quiet neighborhood in Bellevue, Wash., is furnished with everything you’d expect in a multipurpose man cave. There’s a cozy-looking couch situated between a large screen and a digital projector, a Peloton treadmill and a rowing machine. The real showpiece of the space, however, is a custom computer that resembles an oversized erector set, one with seven large Nvidia graphics processing units dangling from its frame.

Flake, a former Microsoft executive and startup founder, built the computer to train custom AI models on terabytes of data from electroencephalograms, the tests that measure electrical activity in the brain—part of a startup project he has since moved on from. To train his AI models, Flake could have paid a cloud service to train them on the industrial-strength GPUs inside their data centers, but he said it was far cheaper to assemble his own machine out of discounted parts (total cost: under $6,000) than to fork over fees to Amazon Web Services or Microsoft every month.

That’s true even when including the $10,000 to $20,000 he spent for electrical upgrades and a new HVAC system he bought to keep his basement cool while his AI computer throws off a lot of heat. “I want to own,” said Flake, who plans to begin using the computer again for a new AI project in the coming months. “I don’t want to rent.”

items.title: Video generation models as world simulators
items.summary: We explore large-scale training of generative models on video data. Specifically, we train text-conditional diffusion models jointly on videos and images of variable durations, resolutions and aspect ratios. We leverage a transformer architecture that operates on spacetime patches of video and image latent codes. Our largest model, Sora, is capable of generating a minute of high fidelity video. Our results suggest that scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world.

mentions.title: Video generation models as world simulators

items.title: Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation
items.summary: We’re developing a blueprint for evaluating the risk that a large language model (LLM) could aid someone in creating a biological threat. In an evaluation involving both biology experts and students, we found that GPT-4 provides at most a mild uplift in biological threat creation accuracy. While this uplift is not large enough to be conclusive, our finding is a starting point for continued research and community deliberation.

items.title: Forecasting potential misuses of language models for disinformation campaigns and how to reduce risk
items.summary: OpenAI researchers collaborated with Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology and the Stanford Internet Observatory to investigate how large language models might be misused for disinformation purposes. The collaboration included an October 2021 workshop bringing together 30 disinformation researchers, machine learning experts, and policy analysts, and culminated in a co-authored report building on more than a year of research. This report outlines the threats that language models pose to the information environment if used to augment disinformation campaigns and introduces a framework for analyzing potential mitigations. Read the full report here.

items.title: Learning to play Minecraft with Video PreTraining
items.summary: We trained a neural network to play Minecraft by Video PreTraining (VPT) on a massive unlabeled video dataset of human Minecraft play, while using only a small amount of labeled contractor data. With fine-tuning, our model can learn to craft diamond tools, a task that usually takes proficient humans over 20 minutes (24,000 actions). Our model uses the native human interface of keypresses and mouse movements, making it quite general, and represents a step towards general computer-using agents.

items.title: AI and efficiency
items.summary: We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012 the amount of compute needed to train a neural net to the same performance on ImageNet classification has been decreasing by a factor of 2 every 16 months. Compared to 2012, it now takes 44 times less compute to train a neural network to the level of AlexNet (by contrast, Moore’s Law would yield an 11x cost improvement over this period). Our results suggest that for AI tasks with high levels of recent investment, algorithmic progress has yielded more gains than classical hardware efficiency.

This report describes 10 mechanisms to improve the verifiability of claims made about AI systems. Developers can use these tools to provide evidence that AI systems are safe, secure, fair, or privacy-preserving. Users, policymakers, and civil society can use these tools to evaluate AI development processes.

items.title: Deep double descent
items.summary: We show that the double descent phenomenon occurs in CNNs, ResNets, and transformers: performance first improves, then gets worse, and then improves again with increasing model size, data size, or training time. This effect is often avoided through careful regularization. While this behavior appears to be fairly universal, we don’t yet fully understand why it happens, and view further study of this phenomenon as an important research direction.

items.title: Solving Rubik’s Cube with a robot hand
items.summary: We’ve trained a pair of neural networks to solve the Rubik’s Cube with a human-like robot hand. The neural networks are trained entirely in simulation, using the same reinforcement learning code as OpenAI Five paired with a new technique called Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR). The system can handle situations it never saw during training, such as being prodded by a stuffed giraffe. This shows that reinforcement learning isn’t just a tool for virtual tasks, but can solve physical-world problems requiring unprecedented dexterity.

items.title: Fine-tuning GPT-2 from human preferences
items.summary: We’ve fine-tuned the 774M parameter GPT-2 language model using human feedback for various tasks, successfully matching the preferences of the external human labelers, though those preferences did not always match our own. Specifically, for summarization tasks the labelers preferred sentences copied wholesale from the input (we’d only asked them to ensure accuracy), so our models learned to copy. Summarization required 60k human labels; simpler tasks which continue text in various styles required only 5k. Our motivation is to move safety techniques closer to the general task of “machines talking to humans,” which we believe is key to extracting information about human values.

mentions.title: Fine-tuning GPT-2 from human preferences

items.title: Emergent tool use from multi-agent interaction
items.summary: We’ve observed agents discovering progressively more complex tool use while playing a simple game of hide-and-seek. Through training in our new simulated hide-and-seek environment, agents build a series of six distinct strategies and counterstrategies, some of which we did not know our environment supported. The self-supervised emergent complexity in this simple environment further suggests that multi-agent co-adaptation may one day produce extremely complex and intelligent behavior.

mentions.title: Emergent tool use from multi-agent interaction

items.title: Testing robustness against unforeseen adversaries
items.summary: We’ve developed a method to assess whether a neural network classifier can reliably defend against adversarial attacks not seen during training. Our method yields a new metric, UAR (Unforeseen Attack Robustness), which evaluates the robustness of a single model against an unanticipated attack, and highlights the need to measure performance across a more diverse range of unforeseen attacks.

mentions.title: Testing robustness against unforeseen adversaries

We’re also releasing an open-source legal agreement to make it easier for organizations to initiate model-sharing partnerships with each other, and are publishing a technical report about our experience in coordinating with the wider AI research community on publication norms.

items.title: Why responsible AI development needs cooperation on safety
items.summary: We’ve written a policy research paper identifying four strategies that can be used today to improve the likelihood of long-term industry cooperation on safety norms in AI: communicating risks and benefits, technical collaboration, increased transparency, and incentivizing standards. Our analysis shows that industry cooperation on safety will be instrumental in ensuring that AI systems are safe and beneficial, but competitive pressures could lead to a collective action problem, potentially causing AI companies to under-invest in safety. We hope these strategies will encourage greater cooperation on the safe development of AI and lead to better global outcomes of AI.

mentions.title: Why responsible AI development needs cooperation on safety

items.title: MuseNet
items.summary: We’ve created MuseNet, a deep neural network that can generate 4-minute musical compositions with 10 different instruments, and can combine styles from country to Mozart to the Beatles. MuseNet was not explicitly programmed with our understanding of music, but instead discovered patterns of harmony, rhythm, and style by learning to predict the next token in hundreds of thousands of MIDI files. MuseNet uses the same general-purpose unsupervised technology as GPT-2, a large-scale transformer model trained to predict the next token in a sequence, whether audio or text.

items.title: OpenAI Five defeats Dota 2 world champions
items.summary: OpenAI Five is the first AI to beat the world champions in an esports game, having won two back-to-back games versus the world champion Dota 2 team, OG, at Finals this weekend. Both OpenAI Five and DeepMind’s AlphaStar had previously beaten good pros privately but lost their live pro matches, making this also the first time an AI has beaten esports pros on livestream.

items.title: Implicit generation and generalization methods for energy-based models
items.summary: We’ve made progress towards stable and scalable training of energy-based models (EBMs) resulting in better sample quality and generalization ability than existing models. Generation in EBMs spends more compute to continually refine its answers and doing so can generate samples competitive with GANs at low temperatures, while also having mode coverage guarantees of likelihood-based models. We hope these findings stimulate further research into this promising class of models.

items.summary: We’ve written a paper arguing that long-term AI safety research needs social scientists to ensure AI alignment algorithms succeed when actual humans are involved. Properly aligning advanced AI systems with human values requires resolving many uncertainties related to the psychology of human rationality, emotion, and biases. The aim of this paper is to spark further collaboration between machine learning and social science researchers, and we plan to hire social scientists to work on this full time at OpenAI.

items.title: How AI training scales
items.summary: We’ve discovered that the gradient noise scale, a simple statistical metric, predicts the parallelizability of neural network training on a wide range of tasks. Since complex tasks tend to have noisier gradients, increasingly large batch sizes are likely to become useful in the future, removing one potential limit to further growth of AI systems. More broadly, these results show that neural network training need not be considered a mysterious art, but can be rigorized and systematized.

We also show cross-domain transfer: we use concepts learned in a 2d particle environment to solve tasks on a 3-dimensional physics-based robot.

items.title: Glow: Better reversible generative models
items.summary: We introduce Glow, a reversible generative model which uses invertible 1x1 convolutions. It extends previous work on reversible generative models and simplifies the architecture. Our model can generate realistic high resolution images, supports efficient sampling, and discovers features that can be used to manipulate attributes of data. items.summary: We’ve trained an agent to achieve a high score of 74,500 on Montezuma’s Revenge from a single human demonstration, better than any previously published result. Our algorithm is simple: the agent plays a sequence of games starting from carefully chosen states from the demonstration, and learns from them by optimizing the game score using PPO, the same reinforcement learning algorithm that underpins OpenAI Five.

items.title: AI and compute
items.summary: We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore’s Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it’s worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today’s capabilities.

items.title: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm
items.summary: We’ve developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.

items.title: More on Dota 2
items.summary: Our Dota 2 result shows that self-play can catapult the performance of machine learning systems from far below human level to superhuman, given sufficient compute. In the span of a month, our system went from barely matching a high-ranked player to beating the top pros and has continued to improve since then. Supervised deep learning systems can only be as good as their training datasets, but in self-play systems, the available data improves automatically as the agent gets better.

items.title: Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate
items.summary: Multiagent environments where agents compete for resources are stepping stones on the path to AGI. Multiagent environments have two useful properties: first, there is a natural curriculum—the difficulty of the environment is determined by the skill of your competitors (and if you’re competing against clones of yourself, the environment exactly matches your skill level). Second, a multiagent environment has no stable equilibrium: no matter how smart an agent is, there’s always pressure to get smarter. These environments have a very different feel from traditional environments, and it’ll take a lot more research before we become good at them.

mentions.title: Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate
